title: The 11-Page Proposal Template + Follow-Up Timing Sheet
description: A page-by-page outline for an 11-page proposal, a follow-up timing sheet built on 742,137 proposals, and how to revise without cutting your price.
lead: This is the full 11-page proposal template and follow-up timing sheet from the reel. Most proposals are opened fast and decided fast. This guide gives you what goes on each of the 11 pages, exactly when to follow up after they open it, and how to handle revisions without discounting.
insider: Proposals come after the calls we book. For a construction software client we booked **31 sales-qualified demos, and their team signed 6 annual contracts**, 5 of them in the last 2 weeks. A fast, clear proposal is what turns a good call into a signed deal. Filling the calendar with calls worth a proposal, every day, is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: [Proposify's State of Proposals 2026](https://www.proposify.com/state-of-proposals-2026) looked at **742,137 proposals** sent in 2025. Four numbers matter most for closing faster:

head: Finding
Number
What it means for you
rows: Time from sending to first open
Buyers open it almost right away
Time from first open to closed-won
Winning deals are decided fast, so follow up the same day
Revisions are a buying signal, not a bad sign

blocks.text: These come from proposals sent through Proposify, so treat them as a strong guide, not a law. The revision numbers show deals with revisions closed more often. They don't prove revisions cause the win, but they do show a buyer asking for changes is usually still in the game.
One idea per page. If a page doesn't help them say yes, cut it.

head: Page
What goes on it
Tip
rows: Their logo and name first, then yours. Project name and date
Make it about them from page one
Their problem in their own words, from the call
2 to 3 results they want, with numbers and dates
"20 booked calls a month by March", not "more leads"
What the problem costs each month it isn't fixed
How you'll get there, in 3 to 5 plain steps
1 case study close to their industry, with real numbers
One strong case beats five weak ones
The people, what they do, how you'll communicate
Name a single point of contact
Price, what's included, payment terms. 2 to 3 options if it fits
Options change scope, not the same work at a lower price
What happens after they sign, start date, signature box

blocks.label: Why e-sign on page 11
blocks.text: Proposify found proposals with e-signatures had a **15% higher close rate** and closed **60% faster**. Make signing a click, not a printer job.
Use the open notification (most proposal tools send one) to time your follow-ups. Don't wait a week to "give them space". The average win is decided about 2.5 days after the first open.

What to do
Message
rows: Agree a decision date on the call
"If it looks right, when would you want to decide?"
Send with a short note, not a long email

Answer a question they're likely to have, or share one more proof point
They open it again, or forward it

blocks.text: **Why the team walkthrough:** Proposify found close rates were **20% higher** when more than one stakeholder viewed the proposal. If others are reading it, help them understand it.

items: Tuesday 10:34: they open it, right on the 34-minute average.
Tuesday 3:00 pm: you send the same-day follow-up: "Any questions so far?"
Thursday evening is 2.5 days after the first open (10:34 Tuesday + 60 hours). That's the average gap to a win, so your day 2 to 3 follow-up goes out Thursday morning.
If there's no reply, the day 7 check goes out the next Tuesday.

blocks.text: Revisions: change scope or timeline, keep the price
When a buyer asks for changes, they are still interested. The mistake is answering "can you do it cheaper?" with a lower price for the same work. Change what they get or when they get it instead.

head: They say
Don't
Do
rows: Remove one deliverable, or start with a smaller first phase
Narrow the scope to hit the date, or price the rush
Add it as an option with its own price
Show what's included that others may not include

blocks.text: Example: a $12,000 proposal for 3 months. Budget is $9,000. Instead of 25% off, offer the same monthly fee for a 2-month first phase ($8,000), with month 3 after they've seen results. Same price per month. Smaller first step.

blocks.label: 11-page proposal prompt
blocks.text:
Here are my notes from the sales call:
[paste notes: their problem in their words, goals, numbers, budget hints, decision date, who else decides]

What I sell: [one sentence]. Price: [price and terms].
Case study to use: [short summary with real numbers].

Write an 11-page proposal outline with these pages: 1 Cover, 2 Their situation, 3 Goals, 4 Cost of waiting, 5 Approach, 6 Scope (included / not included), 7 Timeline, 8 Proof, 9 Who does the work, 10 Investment, 11 Next steps + sign.
Rules: use their words where you can, one idea per page, plain simple English, no made-up numbers. Mark anything I need to fill in as [TO FILL].

blocks.label: Same-day follow-up
blocks.text:
Hi [first name],

Saw you had a chance to open the proposal. Any questions so far?

If it helps, I can walk you and [other person] through it in 15 minutes. Thursday at 10 work?

[your name]

head: Mistake
Fix
rows: Waiting a week to follow up
Same day as the first open, then day 2 to 3
Ask for it on the call, before you send
Change scope or timeline, keep the price
Price on page 3 with no context
Price on page 10, after the goals, plan and proof

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: Send short. Follow up the same day. Change the scope, keep the price.

faq.q: Does my proposal have to be exactly 11 pages?
faq.a: No. 11 was the average for winning proposals in Proposify's data. The real lesson is: shorter and clearer beats longer. If you can say it in 8, do.

faq.q: Isn't following up the same day pushy?
faq.a: Not if it's a short, helpful question. The average win is decided about 2.5 days after the first open, so waiting a week often means you're too late.

faq.q: What if I don't have proposal software with open tracking?
faq.a: Follow up the same day you send it, then on day 2 to 3. Or ask on the call: "When will you have time to read it?"

faq.q: Should I ever lower the price?
faq.a: Only in exchange for something: a smaller scope, payment upfront or a longer term. Never for the same work.
